2	
3	**Course:** STATS 101 (introductory, first-year undergraduate, no prior statistics)
4	**Class length:** 50 minutes
5	**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra
6	
7	## Learning objectives
8	
9	By the end of this module students can:
10	
11	1. Explain what statistics is for and tell a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
12	2. Classify variables (categorical or numerical) and their level of measurement.
13	3. Describe how data are collected (observational study or experiment, sampling methods) and spot common biases.
14	4. Choose a suitable graph for a variable.
15	5. Calculate and interpret measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, IQR, standard deviation).
16	6. Find outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule, compute z-scores and use the 68–95–99.7 rule.
17	7. Explain why correlation does not imply causation.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 1. Why statistics?
22	
23	- Statistics is the science of **collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data** in the presence of variation and uncertainty.
24	- Two branches:
25	  - **Descriptive statistics** summarise the data we have (tables, graphs, averages). Most of this module.
26	  - **Inferential statistics** use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty. Later modules.
27	- Everyday examples: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, A/B tests on websites.
28	- The three questions that structure this module:
29	  1. **Where do the data come from?** (populations, samples, study design)
30	  2. **What kind of data are they?** (types of variables)
31	  3. **What do the data say?** (graphs, centre, spread, shape)
32	
33	## 2. Two stories about data
34	
35	**John Snow, London, 1854.** During a cholera outbreak in Soho, Snow marked each death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed. A simple picture of data pointed to the cause.
36	
37	**The Literary Digest poll, 1936.** The magazine mailed about 10 million ballots, drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states. George Gallup, with a much smaller but better-chosen sample (about 50,000 people), correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.
38	
39	Takeaway: **a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.** How data are collected matters more than how much there is.
40	
41	## 3. Population, sample, parameter, statistic
42	
43	- **Population**: the entire group we want to know about (e.g. all students at the university).
44	- **Sample**: the part of the population we actually collect data from (e.g. 200 students who answered a survey).
45	- **Parameter**: a number describing the population (usually unknown). Notation: population mean **μ**, population standard deviation **σ**.
46	- **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter. Notation: sample mean **x̄**, sample standard deviation **s**.
47	- Memory aid: **P**opulation – **P**arameter; **S**ample – **S**tatistic.
48	
49	## 4. Types of variables
50	
51	| Type | Subtype | What it is | Examples |
52	|---|---|---|---|
53	| Categorical | Nominal | categories with no order | blood type, favourite colour, country |
54	| Categorical | Ordinal | categories with a natural order | satisfaction (low/medium/high), year of study |
55	| Numerical | Discrete | counts, whole numbers | number of siblings, goals scored |
56	| Numerical | Continuous | measurements on a scale | height, time, temperature |
57	
58	Watch out: numbers are not always numerical data. A postcode or a student ID is categorical; averaging them means nothing.
59	
60	## 5. Levels of measurement
61	
62	| Level | Order? | Equal intervals? | True zero? | Example |
63	|---|---|---|---|---|
64	| Nominal | no | no | no | eye colour |
65	| Ordinal | yes | no | no | race finishing position |
66	| Interval | yes | yes | no | temperature in °C |
67	| Ratio | yes | yes | yes | weight, income, time |
68	
69	Why it matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C (interval, no true zero), but 20 kg is twice 10 kg (ratio).
70	
71	## 6. Collecting data: observational studies and experiments
72	
73	- **Observational study**: researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments (e.g. surveying students about sleep and grades). It can show an association, but not cause and effect.
74	- **Experiment**: researchers **assign** treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use:
75	  - a **control group** for comparison,
76	  - **random assignment** to groups, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment,
77	  - a **placebo** where possible, and **blinding** (double-blind: neither subjects nor researchers know who got what).
78	- Only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish **cause and effect**.
79	
80	## 7. Sampling methods
81	
82	| Method | How it works | Example |
83	|---|---|---|
84	| Simple random sample | every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen | draw 100 student IDs at random |
85	| Stratified sample | split into groups (strata), take a random sample from each | 25 students from each year of study |
86	| Cluster sample | split into groups, randomly choose whole groups | randomly pick 5 lecture sections, survey everyone in them |
87	| Systematic sample | choose every k-th individual from a list after a random start | every 20th name on the class list |
88	| Convenience sample | whoever is easiest to reach (**not random; avoid**) | asking friends in the cafeteria |
89	
90	## 8. Bias: when samples mislead
91	
92	- **Selection bias**: the way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population (the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936).
93	- **Non-response bias**: the people who don't respond differ from those who do.
94	- **Response bias**: the question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer ("Don't you agree that…?").
95	- **Voluntary response bias**: only people with strong opinions choose to take part (online polls, call-in shows).
96	- A bigger sample does **not** fix bias; it only makes a biased answer look more precise.
97	
98	## 9. Graphs: picking the right one
99	
100	| Data | Graph | What it shows |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| One categorical variable | bar chart (or pie chart) | counts or percentages per category |
103	| One numerical variable | histogram | shape of the distribution |
104	| One numerical variable | box plot | five-number summary and outliers |
105	| Two numerical variables | scatter plot | relationship (direction, form, strength) |
106	| A variable over time | line graph | trends |
107	
108	Rule: **always plot the data before computing anything.**
109	
110	**Anscombe's quartet (1973):** four small data sets (11 points each) with almost the same mean of x (9), mean of y (about 7.50), correlation (about 0.816) and regression line (y = 3 + 0.5x), yet completely different scatter plots: one straight-line cloud, one curve, one line with a single outlier, one vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story.
111	
112	## 10. Describing a distribution: shape, centre, spread
113	
114	Every description of a numerical variable covers:
115	
116	- **Shape**: symmetric, skewed right (long tail to the right, e.g. incomes), skewed left; one peak (unimodal) or two (bimodal).
117	- **Centre**: where the typical value is.
118	- **Spread**: how much values vary.
119	- **Unusual features**: outliers, gaps.
120	
121	## 11. Measures of centre
122	
123	- **Mean**: add the values and divide by how many. x̄ = Σx / n
124	- **Median**: the middle value of the ordered data (average of the two middle values if n is even).
125	- **Mode**: the most frequent value.
126	
127	**Worked example.** Commute times (minutes) for 10 students:
128	
129	> 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76
130	
131	- Sum = 260, n = 10 → **mean = 26 minutes**
132	- Ordered middle values are 20 and 22 → **median = 21 minutes**
133	- **Mode = 15 minutes** (appears twice)
134	
135	Remove the 76-minute commute: the mean drops to about **20.4**, the median only to **20**.
136	
137	- The median is **resistant** to outliers; the mean is not.
138	- In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median (mean > median); in a left-skewed one, below.
139	- Use the median for skewed data (house prices, incomes); the mean for roughly symmetric data.
140	
141	## 12. Measures of spread
142	
143	- **Range** = maximum − minimum. Commute example: 76 − 12 = **64 minutes**. Very sensitive to outliers.
144	- **Quartiles**: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half.
145	  Commute example: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 → **Q1 = 15**; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 → **Q3 = 27**.
146	- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15 = **12 minutes**: the spread of the middle 50%.
147	- **Standard deviation (s)**: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.
148	
149	> s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )
150	
151	  Commute example: variance ≈ 341.3, **s ≈ 18.5 minutes**. Without the 76-minute value, s ≈ 6.1: one outlier triples the SD.
152	- We divide by n − 1 (not n) for a sample; this corrects for the sample mean being closer to the data than the true mean.
153	
154	## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers
155	
156	- **Five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
157	  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
158	- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
159	  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.
160	- A **box plot** draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers (here 12 and 30), and outliers as separate dots (here 76).
161	
162	## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?
163	
164	> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation
165	
166	- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
167	- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.
168	- z-scores let us compare values on different scales (e.g. a score on a hard test vs an easy one).
169	
170	## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule
171	
172	For data with a roughly **normal (bell-shaped)** distribution:
173	
174	- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
175	- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
176	- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.
177	
178	Exam example (mean 70, SD 8): about 68% of scores between **62 and 78**, about 95% between **54 and 86**, about 99.7% between **46 and 94**. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class.
179	
180	The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.
181	
182	## 16. Correlation is not causation
183	
184	- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
185	- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
186	- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
187	- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.
188	
189	## 17. Summary
190	
191	1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
192	2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
193	3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
194	4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
195	5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
196	6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
197	7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
198	8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
199	9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.
200	
201	**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.
202	
203	## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)
204	
205	1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
206	2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
207	3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
208	4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
209	5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*
210	6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning? *(Answer: no; hot weather is a confounding variable)*
211	
212	## Glossary
213	
214	- **Bias** — a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction.
215	- **Confounding variable** — a third variable that affects both variables being studied.
216	- **IQR** — interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.
217	- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.
218	- **Parameter** — a number describing a population.
219	- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
220	- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
221	- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

> s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )

- We divide by n − 1 (not n) for a sample; this corrects for the sample mean being closer to the data than the true mean.

## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers

- **Five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.
- A **box plot** draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers (here 12 and 30), and outliers as separate dots (here 76).

## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?

> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation

- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.
- z-scores let us compare values on different scales (e.g. a score on a hard test vs an easy one).

## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule

For data with a roughly **normal (bell-shaped)** distribution:

- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.

Exam example (mean 70, SD 8): about 68% of scores between **62 and 78**, about 95% between **54 and 86**, about 99.7% between **46 and 94**. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class.

The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.

## 16. Correlation is not causation

- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.

## 17. Summary

1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.

**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.

## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)

1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*
6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning? *(Answer: no; hot weather is a confounding variable)*

## Glossary

- **Bias** — a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction.
- **Confounding variable** — a third variable that affects both variables being studied.
- **IQR** — interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.
- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.
- **Parameter** — a number describing a population.
- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

1	# The outline (PLAN.md)
2	
3	The contract between planning and building. Whoever builds the deck follows it slide by slide, and the review compares the
4	finished deck against it, so every field is concrete: no "TBD" except facts the user still has to supply.
5	
6	## Format
7	
8	```markdown
9	# <Deck title>
10	
11	- **Audience**: who, and what they already know
12	- **Occasion and time**: event, slot in minutes, whether Q&A is inside the slot
13	- **Goal**: what the audience should know, decide or do at the end
14	- **Promise**: By the end you will ... (said on slide 1 or 2)
15	- **Story**: the whole argument in one sentence
16	- **Fence**: what the idea is not (the nearest alternative it could be confused with)
17	- **Look**: data-theme, data-fonts (empty = the theme's own), lang/dir, one line on why
18	- **Sources**: each file or link used, one per line
19	- **Placeholders**: facts still missing, or "none"
20	
21	| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
22	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
23	| 1 | start | title | ... | subtitle = the promise | promise | 0.5 |
24	| 2 | agenda | agenda | ... | the parts | signpost | 0.5 |
25	| ... |
26	| n | close | closing | ... | what the audience now has, or the ask | contribution | 1 |
27	
28	**Total**: n slides, about N minutes (finish at 85 to 90% of the slot when Q&A is inside it).
29	**Restatements of the story**: slides a, b, c (three, said three different ways).
30	```
31	
32	## Rules for filling it in
33	
34	- **Claim**: a sentence that states something ("Revenue grew 18%"), not a topic ("Revenue"). The titles alone, read in
35	  order, tell the story.
36	- **Content and facts**: only from the user's material, each with its source; anything missing is a named placeholder.
37	- **Role**, one or more per slide: promise, signpost, thesis (a restatement of the story), fence, evidence, story (an
38	  example or case that makes a number tangible), question (to the room), contribution, backup.
39	- **Layout**: one from `references/looks.md`; no more than two bullet slides in a row.

# The outline (PLAN.md)

The contract between planning and building. Whoever builds the deck follows it slide by slide, and the review compares the
finished deck against it, so every field is concrete: no "TBD" except facts the user still has to supply.

## Format

```markdown
# <Deck title>

- **Audience**: who, and what they already know
- **Occasion and time**: event, slot in minutes, whether Q&A is inside the slot
- **Goal**: what the audience should know, decide or do at the end
- **Promise**: By the end you will ... (said on slide 1 or 2)
- **Story**: the whole argument in one sentence
- **Fence**: what the idea is not (the nearest alternative it could be confused with)
- **Look**: data-theme, data-fonts (empty = the theme's own), lang/dir, one line on why
- **Sources**: each file or link used, one per line
- **Placeholders**: facts still missing, or "none"

| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | start | title | ... | subtitle = the promise | promise | 0.5 |
| 2 | agenda | agenda | ... | the parts | signpost | 0.5 |
| ... |
| n | close | closing | ... | what the audience now has, or the ask | contribution | 1 |

**Total**: n slides, about N minutes (finish at 85 to 90% of the slot when Q&A is inside it).
**Restatements of the story**: slides a, b, c (three, said three different ways).
```

## Rules for filling it in

- **Claim**: a sentence that states something ("Revenue grew 18%"), not a topic ("Revenue"). The titles alone, read in
  order, tell the story.
- **Content and facts**: only from the user's material, each with its source; anything missing is a named placeholder.
- **Role**, one or more per slide: promise, signpost, thesis (a restatement of the story), fence, evidence, story (an
  example or case that makes a number tangible), question (to the room), contribution, backup.
- **Layout**: one from `references/looks.md`; no more than two bullet slides in a row.
- **Minutes**: about one per slide for a talk, 1.5 to 2 for a lecture; the total fits the slot.
- **Required roles**: a promise in slides 1 to 2, the story restated three times, a fence, a contribution or the ask
  as the last slide (never "Thank you" or "Questions?"), and signposts when the talk is longer than about 10 minutes.
- Backup slides go last with role `backup`; they start with an appendix slide and are not counted in the time.

STATS 101 · Module 1

Data, samples and describing data

By the end you can tell a population from a sample, choose a graph, describe a data set, find its outliers, and explain why correlation is not causation.

Lecture, 50 minutesFirst year, no statistics background

(About 1 minute.) Welcome. Read the promise on screen aloud: by the end of this lecture you can do seven things, and they all come from the module's learning objectives. Say that no statistics is needed, only high-school algebra. Set the tone: data are messy, and the job is to look at them carefully before trusting any number.

Three questions, then a quiz

  1. Where do the data come from? about 15 min
  2. What kind of data are they? about 7 min
  3. What do the data say? about 22 min
  4. Quiz and summary about 5 min

(About 1 minute.) The module is organised around three questions: where the data come from, what kind of data they are, and what they say. Those three questions return as the three parts of the lecture. Times add up to about 50 minutes, with the quiz at the end so everyone can check their understanding before the summary.

Why statistics?

Statistics is the science of collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data.

It works in the presence of variation and uncertainty.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the main idea, first of three times we say it. Give the everyday examples from the module: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, and A/B tests on websites. Then name the two branches. Descriptive statistics summarises the data we have, with tables, graphs and averages; most of this module is descriptive. Inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty; that comes in later modules.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A map of deaths pointed to the cause

In 1854 John Snow marked each cholera death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the first of two stories. The lesson is that a simple picture of the data pointed to the cause. Snow did not start with a formula; he plotted the deaths and looked. That is the first habit of this module: plot the data before computing anything. Use the image placeholder for Snow's map; a public-domain reproduction is fine, and check the licence before using it.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A huge biased sample is worse than a small, good one

  • 1936: about 10 million ballots mailed, about 2.4 million returned.
  • Drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists.
  • It predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won about 61% and 46 of 48 states.
  • George Gallup's sample of about 50,000 correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.

(About 2 minutes.) The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots and got about 2.4 million back, and its prediction was wrong. Its list came mostly from telephone directories and car-registration lists, which left out poorer voters. Gallup used a much smaller sample, about 50,000 people, chosen better, and was right. Takeaway: how data are collected matters more than how much there is. Repeat it: a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.

Part 1 · Vocabulary

We want to know the population; we only measure a sample

(About 2 minutes.) Three clicks: the population, then the sample, then the arrow. A population is the entire group we want to know about. A sample is the part we actually collected data from. A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic is computed from the sample and used to estimate the parameter. Notation: population mean μ and population standard deviation σ; sample mean x̄ and sample standard deviation s. Memory aid: Population goes with Parameter, Sample goes with Statistic.

Part 1 · Sampling

Random samples spread across the population; convenience samples clump

(About 1.5 minutes.) Each grid is a population of 40 people, and the bright dots are the sample. On the left, the sample was chosen by chance, so it is spread across the whole population. On the right, the sample is whoever was easiest to reach, so it clumps in one corner. Ask the room: which picture is more like the population? The next slide names the five sampling methods.

Part 1 · Sampling methods

Four methods use chance; convenience sampling is the one to avoid

How it worksExample
Simple randomevery group of n individuals has the same chancedraw 100 student IDs at random
Stratifiedsplit into groups, then sample randomly from each25 students from each year of study
Clusterrandomly choose whole groups5 lecture sections; survey everyone in them
Systematicevery k-th individual after a random startevery 20th name on the class list
Conveniencenot random; avoidasking friends in the cafeteria

(About 2 minutes.) Go row by row. Simple random: every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen. Stratified: split the population into groups, called strata, and sample from each. Cluster: randomly choose whole groups and survey everyone in them. Systematic: take every k-th individual from a list after a random start. Convenience: whoever is easiest to reach. It is not random, so avoid it. The cafeteria example is the one to remember.

Part 1 · Bias

Bias: four ways a sample misleads, and size fixes none of them

STATS 101 · Module 1

Data, samples and describing data

By the end you can tell a population from a sample, choose a graph, describe a data set, find its outliers, and explain why correlation is not causation.

Lecture, 50 minutesFirst year, no statistics background

(About 1 minute.) Welcome. Read the promise on screen aloud: by the end of this lecture you can do seven things, and they all come from the module's learning objectives. Say that no statistics is needed, only high-school algebra. Set the tone: data are messy, and the job is to look at them carefully before trusting any number.

Three questions, then a quiz

  1. Where do the data come from? about 15 min
  2. What kind of data are they? about 7 min
  3. What do the data say? about 22 min
  4. Quiz and summary about 5 min

(About 1 minute.) The module is organised around three questions: where the data come from, what kind of data they are, and what they say. Those three questions return as the three parts of the lecture. Times add up to about 50 minutes, with the quiz at the end so everyone can check their understanding before the summary.

Why statistics?

Statistics is the science of collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data.

It works in the presence of variation and uncertainty.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the main idea, first of three times we say it. Give the everyday examples from the module: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, and A/B tests on websites. Then name the two branches. Descriptive statistics summarises the data we have, with tables, graphs and averages; most of this module is descriptive. Inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty; that comes in later modules.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A map of deaths pointed to the cause

In 1854 John Snow marked each cholera death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the first of two stories. The lesson is that a simple picture of the data pointed to the cause. Snow did not start with a formula; he plotted the deaths and looked. That is the first habit of this module: plot the data before computing anything. Use the image placeholder for Snow's map; a public-domain reproduction is fine, and check the licence before using it.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A huge biased sample is worse than a small, good one

  • 1936: about 10 million ballots mailed, about 2.4 million returned.
  • Drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists.
  • It predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won about 61% and 46 of 48 states.
  • George Gallup's sample of about 50,000 correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.

(About 2 minutes.) The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots and got about 2.4 million back, and its prediction was wrong. Its list came mostly from telephone directories and car-registration lists, which left out poorer voters. Gallup used a much smaller sample, about 50,000 people, chosen better, and was right. Takeaway: how data are collected matters more than how much there is. Repeat it: a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.

Part 1 · Vocabulary

We want to know the population; we only measure a sample

(About 2 minutes.) Three clicks: the population, then the sample, then the arrow. A population is the entire group we want to know about. A sample is the part we actually collected data from. A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic is computed from the sample and used to estimate the parameter. Notation: population mean μ and population standard deviation σ; sample mean x̄ and sample standard deviation s. Memory aid: Population goes with Parameter, Sample goes with Statistic.

Part 1 · Sampling

Random samples spread across the population; convenience samples clump

(About 1.5 minutes.) Each grid is a population of 40 people, and the bright dots are the sample. On the left, the sample was chosen by chance, so it is spread across the whole population. On the right, the sample is whoever was easiest to reach, so it clumps in one corner. Ask the room: which picture is more like the population? The next slide names the five sampling methods.

Part 1 · Sampling methods

Four methods use chance; convenience sampling is the one to avoid

How it worksExample
Simple randomevery group of n individuals has the same chancedraw 100 student IDs at random
Stratifiedsplit into groups, then sample randomly from each25 students from each year of study
Clusterrandomly choose whole groups5 lecture sections; survey everyone in them
Systematicevery k-th individual after a random startevery 20th name on the class list
Conveniencenot random; avoidasking friends in the cafeteria

(About 2 minutes.) Go row by row. Simple random: every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen. Stratified: split the population into groups, called strata, and sample from each. Cluster: randomly choose whole groups and survey everyone in them. Systematic: take every k-th individual from a list after a random start. Convenience: whoever is easiest to reach. It is not random, so avoid it. The cafeteria example is the one to remember.

Part 1 · Bias

Bias: four ways a sample misleads, and size fixes none of them

  1. Selection bias

    The way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population.

  2. Non-response bias

    The people who do not respond differ from those who do.

  3. Response bias

    Question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer.

  4. Voluntary response bias

    Only people with strong opinions choose to take part.

  5. A bigger sample does not fix bias

    It only makes a biased answer look more precise.

(About 2 minutes.) Selection bias: the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936. Non-response bias: the people who do not answer differ from those who do. Response bias: a question such as "Don't you agree that...?" pushes people. Voluntary response bias: online polls and call-in shows hear mainly from people with strong opinions. Fence this idea: a bigger sample does not fix bias. It only makes a biased answer look more precise.

Part 1 · Study design

Only a randomised experiment can show cause and effect

Observational study

Researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments, for example by surveying students about sleep and grades.

It can show an association, but not cause and effect.

Experiment

  • Researchers assign the treatments
  • A control group for comparison
  • Random assignment, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment
  • A placebo where possible, and blinding

(About 2 minutes.) The key difference: in an observational study the researchers only observe; in an experiment they assign treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use a control group, random assignment, a placebo where possible, and blinding. Double-blind means neither the subjects nor the researchers know who got which treatment. This is the second of three times we say the main idea: only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish cause and effect.

Part 2 · Types of variables

Every variable is either categorical or numerical

(About 2 minutes.) Build the tree from the top. First question: is the variable categorical, meaning it puts people into groups, or numerical, meaning it is a measurement or a count? Categorical splits into nominal, which have no order, and ordinal, which have a natural order. Numerical splits into discrete, which are counts of whole numbers, and continuous, which are measurements on a scale. Ask the room for one example of each before revealing the examples. Stress the watch-out: a student ID is a number but it is categorical.

Part 2 · Levels of measurement

Only ratio data have order, equal intervals and a true zero

NominalOrdinalIntervalRatio
Order?noyesyesyes
Equal intervals?nonoyesyes
True zero?nononoyes
Exampleeye colourrace finishing positiontemperature in °Cweight, income, time

(About 2 minutes.) Walk across the columns. Nominal: categories with no order, such as eye colour. Ordinal: order, but the gaps are not equal, such as race finishing position. Interval: order and equal intervals, but no true zero, such as temperature in degrees Celsius. Ratio: all three, such as weight, income or time. The next slide shows why the true zero matters.

Why it matters

20 °C is not twice as hot as 10 °C. 20 kg is twice 10 kg.

Interval data have no true zero; ratio data do.

(About 1 minute.) This is the reason the levels matter. Temperature in degrees Celsius is an interval scale: zero degrees is not the absence of temperature, so 20 °C is not twice as hot as 10 °C. Weight is a ratio scale: zero kilograms is no weight at all, so 20 kg really is twice 10 kg. Before you say that a value is twice another, check the level of measurement.

Part 3 · Graphs

Plot before you compute, using the graph that fits the variable

DataGraphWhat it shows
One categorical variablebar chart (or pie chart)counts or percentages per category
One numerical variablehistogramthe shape of the distribution
One numerical variablebox plotfive-number summary and outliers
Two numerical variablesscatter plotrelationship: direction, form, strength
A variable over timeline graphtrends

(About 1.5 minutes.) Read the table as a lookup. Match the kind of variable to the graph, then to what it shows. The rule underneath is the most important line in this part: always plot the data before computing anything. The box plot is the graph we use for outliers later in the lecture.

Part 3 · Always plot first

Same summary numbers, four completely different pictures

9mean of x in each data set
7.50mean of y, about
0.816correlation, about
0.5slope of the regression line, y = 3 + 0.5x

Anscombe's quartet (1973): four data sets of 11 points each

(About 2 minutes.) Anscombe's quartet is four small data sets with almost the same summary numbers: the same mean of x, the same mean of y, the same correlation and the same regression line. Their scatter plots are completely different: one is a straight-line cloud, one is a curve, one is a line with a single outlier, and one is a vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story, so plot first.

Part 3 · Shape and centre

Right skew pulls the mean above the median

(About 2 minutes.) Every numerical distribution is described by its shape, centre, spread and unusual features. The left curve is roughly symmetric, so the mean and median coincide. The right curve has a long tail to the right, as incomes do; the tail pulls the mean up above the median. These curves are illustrations of shape only, with no data behind them.

Part 3 · Centre

The mean shares out the total; the median takes the middle

x̄ = Σx / n
Σx
add all the values
n
how many values
Median
middle of the ordered data; average the two middle values if n is even
Mode
the most frequent value

(About 2 minutes.) The mean is x̄ = Σx / n: add the values and divide by how many there are. The median is the middle value of the ordered data, and when n is even it is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the most frequent value. Next we apply all three to ten real commute times.

Worked example · commute times

Ten commutes give three different centres

26minmean: 260 ÷ 10
21minmedian: average of 20 and 22
15minmode: appears twice

Commute times in minutes, 10 students: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76

(About 2 minutes.) Work it on the board with the class. The values sum to 260, so the mean is 26 minutes. Sorted, the two middle values are 20 and 22, so the median is 21. The mode is 15, the only value that appears twice. Point out the 76: it is the reason the mean sits above most of the commutes.

Part 3 · Outliers and centre

One 76-minute commute moves the mean, but barely the median

All ten commutesWithout the 76
Mean26 minabout 20.4 min
Median21 min20 min

(About 1.5 minutes.) Remove the 76-minute commute and the mean drops from 26 to about 20.4, while the median only drops from 21 to 20. The median is resistant to outliers; the mean is not. In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median, and for skewed data such as house prices or incomes, use the median.

Part 3 · Spread

The outlier stretches the range; the IQR covers the middle 50%

64minrange: 76 − 12
12minIQR: Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15
18.5minstandard deviation, s

Quartiles: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 gives Q1 = 15; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 gives Q3 = 27

(About 2 minutes.) Range is the maximum minus the minimum: 76 minus 12, which is 64 minutes, and very sensitive to the outlier. Q1 is the median of the lower half, 15; Q3 is the median of the upper half, 27. The IQR, Q3 minus Q1, is 12 minutes and is the spread of the middle 50%. Standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of values from the mean: about 18.5 minutes here.

Part 3 · Standard deviation

One 76-minute outlier triples the standard deviation

s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )
x̄
the sample mean
n − 1
for a sample we divide by n − 1, not n; this corrects for the sample mean sitting closer to the data than the true mean

With the 76: s ≈ 18.5 min. Without it: s ≈ 6.1 min.

(About 2 minutes.) Read the formula in words: for each value, take its distance from the mean and square it, add those up, divide by n minus 1, then take the square root. The variance, before the square root, is about 341.3 for the ten commutes, so s is about 18.5 minutes. Without the 76 the standard deviation is about 6.1 minutes: one outlier roughly triples it. This is the same lesson as the mean and range.

Part 3 · Outliers

The 1.5 × IQR rule flags the 76-minute commute

(About 2.5 minutes.) The five-number summary is minimum 12, Q1 15, median 21, Q3 27 and maximum 76. Draw the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median. The whiskers run to the most extreme values that are not outliers, 12 and 30. The 1.5 × IQR rule: with IQR 12, 1.5 × 12 = 18, so the fences are 15 − 18 = −3 and 27 + 18 = 45. The 76 lies beyond 45, so it is a suspected outlier. Click through the builds slowly.

Part 3 · z-scores

A z-score says how many SDs a value sits from the mean

z = (x − mean) / SD
x
the value we are looking at
SD
the standard deviation of the data

Exam: mean 70, SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = 2: two SDs above the mean.

(About 2 minutes.) A z-score is the number of standard deviations a value lies above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. Worked example: an exam with mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = 2. z-scores also let us compare values on different scales, such as a score on a hard test and a score on an easy one.

Part 3 · Bell-shaped data

For bell-shaped data, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs

(About 2.5 minutes.) Build the bell, then the three brackets from the inside out. About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SDs and about 99.7% within 3 SDs. In the exam, that means scores of 62 to 78, 54 to 86 and 46 to 94. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class. Warn them: the rule does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.

Part 3 · Correlation

Ice cream does not cause drownings; hot weather drives both

(About 2.5 minutes.) Ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together across a year, so they are correlated. Ice cream does not cause drowning. Hot weather drives both, and it is a confounding variable: a third variable that affects both things being studied. Other reasons for a correlation without causation are reverse causation and coincidence. The only way to show cause and effect is a randomised experiment. This is the third time we say the main idea, and the fence: correlation is not causation.

Quiz · 1 of 3

Check your understanding

1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level?

Categorical, nominal

2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem?

Selection bias from a convenience sample: gym-goers exercise more than the population.

(About 2 minutes.) Give the room 30 seconds per question before you click. Question 1: a colour has no order, so it is categorical and nominal. Question 2: a gym is not random, so this is a convenience sample, and the people in it differ from the population. Click to reveal the answers.

Quiz · 2 of 3

Check your understanding

3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10.

Mean 5, median 4

4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median?

The median

(About 2 minutes.) Question 3: the values sum to 25, so the mean is 5; the middle value of the ordered list is 4. Question 4: the median is resistant to outliers, the mean is not. Click to reveal.

Quiz · 3 of 3

Check your understanding

5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82?

1.5, since (82 − 70) / 8 = 1.5

6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning?

No. Hot weather is a confounding variable.

(About 2 minutes.) Question 5 is a direct use of the z-score formula. Question 6 is the fence: correlation is not causation. Click to reveal, then move to the summary.

Summary

Collect carefully, plot first, then describe with centre and spread

  1. Design matters more than size

    Random sampling and randomised experiments. A bigger biased sample does not help.

  2. Know the variable

    Categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).

  3. Plot before you compute

    Anscombe's quartet: the same summary numbers, four different pictures.

  4. Centre and spread

    Mean (sensitive) or median (resistant); range, IQR, SD; outliers beyond 1.5 × IQR.

  5. Correlation is not causation

    Look for confounders. Next module: probability, the language of uncertainty.

(About 1 minute.) This is the third and final time we say the main idea: collect carefully, plot first, then describe with centre and spread. Walk the five rows quickly. Next module is probability, the language of uncertainty. You now know how to ask where data come from, what kind they are and what they say; that is the foundation for everything that follows. Good luck with the next module, and see you there.

Data, samples and describing data

By the end you can tell a population from a sample, choose a graph, describe a data set, find its outliers, and explain why correlation is not causation.

(About 1 minute.) Welcome. Read the promise on screen aloud: by the end of this lecture you can do seven things, and they all come from the module's learning objectives. Say that no statistics is needed, only high-school algebra. Set the tone: data are messy, and the job is to look at them carefully before trusting any number.

Three questions, then a quiz

  1. Where do the data come from? about 15 min
  2. What kind of data are they? about 7 min
  3. What do the data say? about 22 min
  4. Quiz and summary about 5 min

(About 1 minute.) The module is organised around three questions: where the data come from, what kind of data they are, and what they say. Those three questions return as the three parts of the lecture. Times add up to about 50 minutes, with the quiz at the end so everyone can check their understanding before the summary.

Why statistics?

Statistics is the science of collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data.

It works in the presence of variation and uncertainty.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the main idea, first of three times we say it. Give the everyday examples from the module: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, and A/B tests on websites. Then name the two branches. Descriptive statistics summarises the data we have, with tables, graphs and averages; most of this module is descriptive. Inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty; that comes in later modules.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A map of deaths pointed to the cause

In 1854 John Snow marked each cholera death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the first of two stories. The lesson is that a simple picture of the data pointed to the cause. Snow did not start with a formula; he plotted the deaths and looked. That is the first habit of this module: plot the data before computing anything. Use the image placeholder for Snow's map; a public-domain reproduction is fine, and check the licence before using it.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A huge biased sample is worse than a small, good one

  • 1936: about 10 million ballots mailed, about 2.4 million returned.
  • Drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists.
  • It predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won about 61% and 46 of 48 states.
  • George Gallup's sample of about 50,000 correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.

(About 2 minutes.) The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots and got about 2.4 million back, and its prediction was wrong. Its list came mostly from telephone directories and car-registration lists, which left out poorer voters. Gallup used a much smaller sample, about 50,000 people, chosen better, and was right. (About 2 minutes.) Three clicks: the population, then the sample, then the arrow. A population is the entire group we want to know about. A sample is the part we actually collected data from. Part 1 · Sampling

Random samples spread across the population; convenience samples clump

(About 1.5 minutes.) Each grid stands for a population, and the bright dots are the sample. On the left, the sample was chosen by chance, so it is spread across the whole population. How it worksExample

(About 2 minutes.) Go row by row. Simple random: every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen. Stratified: split the population into groups, called strata, and sample from each.     The people who do not respond differ from those who do.

  3. What do the data say? about 22 min
  4. Quiz and summary about 5 min

Order?noyesyesyes

STATS 101 · Module 1

Data, samples and describing data

By the end you can tell a population from a sample, choose a graph, describe a data set, find its outliers, and explain why correlation is not causation.

Lecture, 50 minutesFirst year, no statistics background

(About 1 minute.) Welcome. Read the promise on screen aloud: by the end of this lecture you can do seven things, and they all come from the module's learning objectives. Say that no statistics is needed, only high-school algebra. Set the tone: data are messy, and the job is to look at them carefully before trusting any number.

Three questions, then a quiz

  1. Where do the data come from? about 15 min
  2. What kind of data are they? about 7 min
  3. What do the data say? about 22 min
  4. Quiz and summary about 5 min

(About 1 minute.) The module is organised around three questions: where the data come from, what kind of data they are, and what they say. Those three questions return as the three parts of the lecture. Times add up to about 50 minutes, with the quiz at the end so everyone can check their understanding before the summary.

Why statistics?

Statistics is the science of collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data.

It works in the presence of variation and uncertainty.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the main idea, first of three times we say it. Give the everyday examples from the module: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, and A/B tests on websites. Then name the two branches. Descriptive statistics summarises the data we have, with tables, graphs and averages; most of this module is descriptive. Inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty; that comes in later modules.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A map of deaths pointed to the cause

In 1854 John Snow marked each cholera death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed.

(About 2 minutes.) This is the first of two stories. The lesson is that a simple picture of the data pointed to the cause. Snow did not start with a formula; he plotted the deaths and looked. That is the first habit of this module: plot the data before computing anything. Use the image placeholder for Snow's map; a public-domain reproduction is fine, and check the licence before using it.

Part 1 · Where do the data come from?

A huge biased sample is worse than a small, good one

  • 1936: about 10 million ballots mailed, about 2.4 million returned.
  • Drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists.
  • It predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won about 61% and 46 of 48 states.
  • George Gallup's sample of about 50,000 correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.

(About 2 minutes.) The Literary Digest mailed about 10 million ballots and got about 2.4 million back, and its prediction was wrong. Its list came mostly from telephone directories and car-registration lists, which left out poorer voters. Gallup used a much smaller sample, about 50,000 people, chosen better, and was right. Takeaway: how data are collected matters more than how much there is. Repeat it: a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.

Part 1 · Vocabulary

We want to know the population; we only measure a sample

(About 2 minutes.) Three clicks: the population, then the sample, then the arrow. A population is the entire group we want to know about. A sample is the part we actually collected data from. A parameter describes the population and is usually unknown; a statistic is computed from the sample and used to estimate the parameter. Notation: population mean μ and population standard deviation σ; sample mean x̄ and sample standard deviation s. Memory aid: Population goes with Parameter, Sample goes with Statistic.

Part 1 · Sampling

Random samples spread across the population; convenience samples clump

(About 1.5 minutes.) Each grid stands for a population, and the bright dots are the sample. On the left, the sample was chosen by chance, so it is spread across the whole population. On the right, the sample is whoever was easiest to reach, so it clumps in one corner. Ask the room: which picture is more like the population? The next slide names the five sampling methods.

Part 1 · Sampling methods

Four methods use chance; convenience sampling is the one to avoid

How it worksExample
Simple randomevery n-person group has the same chance100 student IDs drawn at random
Stratifiedrandom sample from each group25 students from each year
Clusterrandom whole groups5 lecture sections, all surveyed
Systematicevery k-th after a random startevery 20th name on the list
Conveniencenot random: avoidasking friends in the cafeteria

(About 2 minutes.) Go row by row. Simple random: every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen. Stratified: split the population into groups, called strata, and sample from each. Cluster: randomly choose whole groups and survey everyone in them. Systematic: take every k-th individual from a list after a random start. Convenience: whoever is easiest to reach. It is not random, so avoid it. The cafeteria example is the one to remember.

Part 1 · Bias

Bias: four ways a sample misleads, and size fixes none of them

  1. Selection bias

    The way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population.

  2. Non-response bias

    The people who do not respond differ from those who do.

  3. Response bias

    Question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer.

  4. Voluntary response bias

    Only people with strong opinions choose to take part.

  5. A bigger sample does not fix bias

    It only makes a biased answer look more precise.

(About 2 minutes.) Selection bias: the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936. Non-response bias: the people who do not answer differ from those who do. Response bias: a question such as "Don't you agree that...?" pushes people. Voluntary response bias: online polls and call-in shows hear mainly from people with strong opinions. Fence this idea: a bigger sample does not fix bias. It only makes a biased answer look more precise.

Part 1 · Study design

Only a randomised experiment can show cause and effect

Observational study

Researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments, for example by surveying students about sleep and grades.

It can show an association, but not cause and effect.

Experiment

  • Researchers assign the treatments
  • A control group for comparison
  • Random assignment, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment
  • A placebo where possible, and blinding

(About 2 minutes.) The key difference: in an observational study the researchers only observe; in an experiment they assign treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use a control group, random assignment, a placebo where possible, and blinding. Double-blind means neither the subjects nor the researchers know who got which treatment. This is the second of three times we say the main idea: only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish cause and effect.

Part 2 · Types of variables

Every variable is either categorical or numerical

(About 2 minutes.) Build the tree from the top. First question: is the variable categorical, meaning it puts people into groups, or numerical, meaning it is a measurement or a count? Categorical splits into nominal, which have no order, and ordinal, which have a natural order. Numerical splits into discrete, which are counts of whole numbers, and continuous, which are measurements on a scale. Ask the room for one example of each before revealing the examples. Stress the watch-out: a student ID is a number but it is categorical.

Part 2 · Levels of measurement

Only ratio data have order, equal intervals and a true zero

NominalOrdinalIntervalRatio
Order?noyesyesyes
Equal intervals?nonoyesyes
True zero?nononoyes
Exampleeye colourrace finishing positiontemperature in °Cweight, income, time

(About 2 minutes.) Walk across the columns. Nominal: categories with no order, such as eye colour. Ordinal: order, but the gaps are not equal, such as race finishing position. Interval: order and equal intervals, but no true zero, such as temperature in degrees Celsius. Ratio: all three, such as weight, income or time. The next slide shows why the true zero matters.

Why it matters

20 °C is not twice as hot as 10 °C. 20 kg is twice 10 kg.

Interval data have no true zero; ratio data do.

(About 1 minute.) This is the reason the levels matter. Temperature in degrees Celsius is an interval scale: zero degrees is not the absence of temperature, so 20 °C is not twice as hot as 10 °C. Weight is a ratio scale: zero kilograms is no weight at all, so 20 kg really is twice 10 kg. Before you say that a value is twice another, check the level of measurement.

Part 3 · Graphs

Plot before you compute, using the graph that fits the variable

DataGraphWhat it shows
Categoricalbar chart or pie chartcounts or percentages
Numericalhistogramshape of the distribution
Numericalbox plotfive-number summary, outliers
Two numericalscatter plotdirection, form, strength
Over timeline graphtrends

(About 1.5 minutes.) Read the table as a lookup. Match the kind of variable to the graph, then to what it shows. The rule underneath is the most important line in this part: always plot the data before computing anything. The box plot is the graph we use for outliers later in the lecture.

Part 3 · Always plot first

Same summary numbers, four completely different pictures

9mean of x in each data set
7.50mean of y, about
0.816correlation, about
0.5slope of the regression line, y = 3 + 0.5x

Anscombe's quartet (1973): four data sets of 11 points each

(About 2 minutes.) Anscombe's quartet is four small data sets with almost the same summary numbers: the same mean of x, the same mean of y, the same correlation and the same regression line. Their scatter plots are completely different: one is a straight-line cloud, one is a curve, one is a line with a single outlier, and one is a vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story, so plot first.

Part 3 · Shape and centre

Right skew pulls the mean above the median

(About 2 minutes.) Every numerical distribution is described by its shape, centre, spread and unusual features. The left curve is roughly symmetric, so the mean and median coincide. The right curve has a long tail to the right, as incomes do; the tail pulls the mean up above the median. These curves are illustrations of shape only, with no data behind them.

Part 3 · Centre

The mean shares out the total; the median takes the middle

x̄ = Σx / n
Σx
add all the values
n
how many values
Median
middle of the ordered data; average the two middle values if n is even
Mode
the most frequent value

(About 2 minutes.) The mean is x̄ = Σx / n: add the values and divide by how many there are. The median is the middle value of the ordered data, and when n is even it is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the most frequent value. Next we apply all three to ten real commute times.

Worked example · commute times

Ten commutes give three different centres

26minmean: 260 ÷ 10
21minmedian: average of 20 and 22
15minmode: appears twice

Commute times in minutes, 10 students: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76

(About 2 minutes.) Work it on the board with the class. The values sum to 260, so the mean is 26 minutes. Sorted, the two middle values are 20 and 22, so the median is 21. The mode is 15, the only value that appears twice. Point out the 76: it is the reason the mean sits above most of the commutes.

Part 3 · Outliers and centre

One 76-minute commute moves the mean, but barely the median

All ten commutesWithout the 76
Mean26 minabout 20.4 min
Median21 min20 min

(About 1.5 minutes.) Remove the 76-minute commute and the mean drops from 26 to about 20.4, while the median only drops from 21 to 20. The median is resistant to outliers; the mean is not. In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median, and for skewed data such as house prices or incomes, use the median.

Part 3 · Spread

The outlier stretches the range; the IQR covers the middle 50%

64minrange: 76 − 12
12minIQR: Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15
18.5minstandard deviation, s

Quartiles: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 gives Q1 = 15; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 gives Q3 = 27

(About 2 minutes.) Range is the maximum minus the minimum: 76 minus 12, which is 64 minutes, and very sensitive to the outlier. Q1 is the median of the lower half, 15; Q3 is the median of the upper half, 27. The IQR, Q3 minus Q1, is 12 minutes and is the spread of the middle 50%. Standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of values from the mean: about 18.5 minutes here.

Part 3 · Standard deviation

One 76-minute outlier triples the standard deviation

s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )
x̄
the sample mean
n − 1
for a sample we divide by n − 1, not n; this corrects for the sample mean sitting closer to the data than the true mean

With the 76: s ≈ 18.5 min. Without it: s ≈ 6.1 min.

(About 2 minutes.) Read the formula in words: for each value, take its distance from the mean and square it, add those up, divide by n minus 1, then take the square root. The variance, before the square root, is about 341.3 for the ten commutes, so s is about 18.5 minutes. Without the 76 the standard deviation is about 6.1 minutes: one outlier roughly triples it. This is the same lesson as the mean and range.

Part 3 · Outliers

The 1.5 × IQR rule flags the 76-minute commute

(About 2.5 minutes.) The five-number summary is minimum 12, Q1 15, median 21, Q3 27 and maximum 76. Draw the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median. The whiskers run to the most extreme values that are not outliers, 12 and 30. The 1.5 × IQR rule: with IQR 12, 1.5 × 12 = 18, so the fences are 15 − 18 = −3 and 27 + 18 = 45. The 76 lies beyond 45, so it is a suspected outlier. Click through the builds slowly.

A z-score says how many SDs a value sits from the mean

z = (x − mean) / SD
x
the value we are looking at
SD
the standard deviation of the data

Exam: mean 70, SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = 2: two SDs above the mean.

(About 2 minutes.) A z-score is the number of standard deviations a value lies above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. Worked example: an exam with mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = 2. z-scores also let us compare values on different scales, such as a score on a hard test and a score on an easy one.

Part 3 · Bell-shaped data

For bell-shaped data, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs

(About 2.5 minutes.) Build the bell, then the three brackets from the inside out. About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SDs and about 99.7% within 3 SDs. In the exam, that means scores of 62 to 78, 54 to 86 and 46 to 94. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class. Warn them: the rule does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.

Ice cream does not cause drownings; hot weather drives both

(About 2.5 minutes.) Ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together across a year, so they are correlated. Ice cream does not cause drowning. Hot weather drives both, and it is a confounding variable: a third variable that affects both things being studied. Other reasons for a correlation without causation are reverse causation and coincidence. The only way to show cause and effect is a randomised experiment.
